title: Variations in economic activity: aggregate demand and aggregate supply
summary: AD is total planned spending; AS is total planned output. Their interaction determines real output and the price level. Keynesian and new classical views disagree on whether economies self-correct.

keyterms.definition: Total planned spending on an economy’s goods and services at each price level: C + I + G + (X − M).
Household spending on goods and services; affected by income, wealth, confidence, interest rates and debt.
Spending by firms on capital goods; affected by interest rates, business confidence, technology and taxes.
Total output firms plan to supply at each price level when wages and other input prices are fixed.
Output at full employment; vertical at potential output in the new classical (monetarist) view.
An AS curve that is flat at low output (spare capacity), upward sloping as capacity is approached, and vertical at full employment.
When equilibrium real output is below potential output, so there is cyclical unemployment.
When equilibrium real output is above potential output, pushing up the price level.
A rise in asset prices (houses, shares) makes households feel richer, so consumption rises.
A sudden change in costs (e.g. oil prices) that shifts SRAS.
The idea that flexible wages and prices return the economy to full employment in the long run.

questions.prompt: Why does the AD curve slope downward?
options: Firms supply more at lower prices
Government spends more at lower prices
A lower price level raises real wealth, lowers interest rates and makes exports more competitive
questions.explanation: The wealth, interest-rate and international trade effects explain the slope.

questions.prompt: Match each event to its effect on AD.
questions.explanation: Changes in any component of C + I + G + (X − M) shift AD.

questions.statement: A rise in house prices is likely to increase consumption through the wealth effect.
questions.explanation: Households feel richer and may borrow against higher home values.

questions.text: Spending by firms on capital goods is called ___.
questions.explanation: Investment is the most volatile component of AD.

questions.prompt: A sharp rise in world oil prices will…
options: shift SRAS left, raising the price level and lowering output
questions.explanation: Higher costs reduce the output firms will supply at each price level: a negative supply shock.

questions.prompt: Which shifts LRAS to the right?
options: An improvement in the quality of education and training
A rise in the price level
questions.explanation: LRAS depends on the quantity and quality of factors of production and technology.

questions.statement: In the new classical model, the LRAS curve is vertical at potential output.
questions.explanation: In the long run, output is set by productive capacity, not by the price level.

questions.text: Total output firms plan to supply when input prices are fixed is short-run aggregate ___.
questions.explanation: SRAS slopes upward and shifts with costs of production.

questions.prompt: Which is the most likely result of a fall in AD when the economy is at full employment (new classical view) in the short run?
options: Real output falls below potential and unemployment rises
questions.explanation: In the short run, falling AD reduces output; in the long run wages adjust and SRAS shifts.

questions.prompt: Order the effects of a rise in business confidence.
items: Real output and the price level rise
questions.explanation: Confidence is a key determinant of investment.

lessons.title: Equilibrium, gaps and schools of thought

questions.prompt: When equilibrium output is below potential output, there is…
questions.explanation: Output below potential means cyclical unemployment.

questions.statement: Keynesians argue that an economy can remain in a recessionary gap for a long time.
questions.explanation: Wages are sticky downward and confidence is low, so government action may be needed.

questions.prompt: On the horizontal section of the Keynesian AS curve, a rise in AD causes…
options: a higher price level and no change in output
a fall in the price level
higher output with no rise in the price level
questions.explanation: There is spare capacity, so firms can expand without raising prices.

questions.text: Equilibrium output above potential output creates an ___ gap.
questions.explanation: Excess demand pushes up the price level.

questions.prompt: Match each view to its belief.
questions.explanation: The schools disagree about the speed of self-correction and need for intervention.

questions.prompt: In the new classical model, how does an economy in a recessionary gap return to full employment?
options: Wages and costs fall, shifting SRAS right
questions.explanation: Unemployment puts downward pressure on wages, lowering costs and raising SRAS.

questions.statement: On the vertical section of the Keynesian AS curve, a rise in AD increases only the price level.
questions.explanation: The economy is at full capacity, so extra demand is purely inflationary.

options: Falling output and rising price level, caused by SRAS shifting left
Rising output and rising prices from AD shifting right
Falling output and falling prices from AD shifting left
questions.explanation: A negative supply shock causes both unemployment and inflation.

questions.text: The idea that markets return the economy to full employment unaided is ___-correction.
questions.explanation: New classical economists stress self-correction.

questions.prompt: Order the Keynesian argument for intervention in a recession.
items: AD falls and output drops below potential
Wages are sticky, so the labour market does not clear
Government raises spending to boost AD
questions.explanation: Keynesians see a role for demand management to close recessionary gaps.
